scenes.tts: The first film placed fossil whales in time. If that history is right, what should we find inside living whales and their DNA?
scenes.caption: The first film placed fossil whales in time. If that history is right, what should we find inside living whales and their DNA?
scenes.visual: Reuse the first film's COLOR MAP exactly: rock layers grey, fossils gold, volcanic ash red, DNA blue, anatomy green, development teal, tree white. The carried grey cliff compresses into a timeline beside a large schematic whale tree. Blue, green, and teal question marks move along empty evidence lanes.
scenes.narration: The first film placed fossil whales in time. If that history is right, what should we find inside living whales and their DNA?

scenes.visual: Keep the whale tree dimly visible. Place the title large over it, then dissolve the letters into the four moving evidence lanes.

scenes.tts: Keep one branching tree in view. A common ancestor is an ancestral population from which later species descended. Branches split; they do not form a ladder. Living species sit at the tips.
scenes.caption: Keep one branching tree in view. A common ancestor is an ancestral population from which later species descended. Branches split; they do not form a ladder. Living species sit at the tips.
scenes.visual: Grow one thick white trunk into three branches labeled whale, hippo, and fish. Keep every tip level across the top. Remove a faint ladder icon as the branches spread. Label the tree 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Keep one branching tree in view. A common ancestor is an ancestral population from which later species descended. Branches split; they do not form a ladder. Living species sit at the tips.

scenes.tts: DNA passes from parents to offspring. Small copied changes can travel down a branch. Nearby branches have had less time to collect different changes. Matching DNA stretches are therefore usually more similar.
scenes.caption: DNA passes from parents to offspring. Small copied changes can travel down a branch. Nearby branches have had less time to collect different changes. Matching DNA stretches are therefore usually more similar.
scenes.visual: Run blue block sequences down the white branches. Add a small blue insertion marker once, then copy it toward descendant tips. Keep the alignment large and label it 'schematic DNA blocks'.
scenes.narration: DNA passes from parents to offspring. Small copied changes can travel down a branch. Nearby branches have had less time to collect different changes. Matching DNA stretches are therefore usually more similar.

scenes.tts: Suppose an insertion spread through the ancestral population of whales and hippos before they split, and was never lost. Where should matching markers appear today? Choose whale and hippo, whale and fish, or all three.
scenes.caption: Suppose an insertion spread through the ancestral population of whales and hippos before they split, and was never lost. Where should matching markers appear today? Choose whale and hippo, whale and fish, or all three.
scenes.visual: Show the white tree with one blue insertion at the whale-hippo fork. Place empty blue marker slots beside the three tips and a large question mark above them.
scenes.narration: Suppose an insertion spread through the ancestral population of whales and hippos before they split, and was never lost. Where should matching markers appear today? Choose whale and hippo, whale and fish, or all three.

scenes.visual: Hold the question and empty marker slots. Pulse each possible pair once while the blue insertion glows gently at the shared fork.

scenes.tts: The matching markers should reach whales and hippos. Researchers found shared insertions at the same spots in the genome. That pattern groups whales with hippos among even-toed hoofed mammals.
scenes.caption: The matching markers should reach whales and hippos. Researchers found shared insertions at the same spots in the genome. That pattern groups whales with hippos among even-toed hoofed mammals.
scenes.visual: Animate blue markers from the shared fork to whale and hippo tips only. Replace the question mark with a cautious label, 'fits shared ancestry', and keep the gold fossil timeline visible beside the tree. The other colored evidence lanes begin moving.
scenes.narration: The matching markers should reach whales and hippos. Researchers found shared insertions at the same spots in the genome. That pattern groups whales with hippos among even-toed hoofed mammals.

scenes.tts: That grouping does not mean hippos became whales. Both living groups occupy separate tips. They share an earlier population, then each branch continued changing. Relatives are not automatically ancestors.
scenes.caption: That grouping does not mean hippos became whales. Both living groups occupy separate tips. They share an earlier population, then each branch continued changing. Relatives are not automatically ancestors.
scenes.visual: Keep whale and hippo on separate white tips. Move both outward from their shared fork at the same speed. Cross out a temporary arrow pointing from the hippo tip toward the whale tip.
scenes.narration: That grouping does not mean hippos became whales. Both living groups occupy separate tips. They share an earlier population, then each branch continued changing. Relatives are not automatically ancestors.

scenes.tts: Anatomy tests the tree another way. Homologous structures come from one structure in a common ancestor. A whale flipper, a human arm and a bat wing hold the same set of bones, arranged differently.
scenes.caption: Anatomy tests the tree another way. Homologous structures come from one structure in a common ancestor. A whale flipper, a human arm and a bat wing hold the same set of bones, arranged differently.
scenes.visual: The tree shifts left but stays visible. On the right, one large schematic green set of labeled bone blocks smoothly reshapes into flipper, arm, and wing outlines without drawing molecular structures.
scenes.narration: Anatomy tests the tree another way. Homologous structures come from one structure in a common ancestor. A whale flipper, a human arm and a bat wing hold the same set of bones, arranged differently.

scenes.tts: Living whales also carry small hip bones that support no legs. They are vestigial: reduced parts that have lost all or most of the job they did in ancestors. Vestigial does not mean useless. In males, these bones anchor muscles used in mating.
scenes.caption: Living whales also carry small hip bones that support no legs. They are vestigial: reduced parts that have lost all or most of the job they did in ancestors. Vestigial does not mean useless. In males, these bones anchor muscles used in mating.
scenes.visual: Morph the flipper outline into a full-height whale silhouette. Two small green hip-bone blocks glow inside, with no legs attached. A simple green muscle band attaches while the label changes from 'leg support' to 'muscle anchor'.
scenes.narration: Living whales also carry small hip bones that support no legs. They are vestigial: reduced parts that have lost all or most of the job they did in ancestors. Vestigial does not mean useless. In males, these bones anchor muscles used in mating.

scenes.tts: Development supplies a fourth test. A spotted dolphin embryo begins hind-limb buds. The signals that keep a limb growing switch off early or never appear. The buds stop and break down. The embryo is not replaying its ancestors.
scenes.caption: Development supplies a fourth test. A spotted dolphin embryo begins hind-limb buds. The signals that keep a limb growing switch off early or never appear. The buds stop and break down. The embryo is not replaying its ancestors.
scenes.visual: Transform the whale into one large schematic dolphin embryo. Teal buds grow briefly, pause, then shrink. Keep the earlier stage as a faint outline beside the later stage, connected by a development arrow.
scenes.narration: Development supplies a fourth test. A spotted dolphin embryo begins hind-limb buds. The signals that keep a limb growing switch off early or never appear. The buds stop and break down. The embryo is not replaying its ancestors.

scenes.tts: Now bring the lanes together. Gold fossils show change through time. Blue DNA places whales on a mammal branch. Green anatomy and teal development preserve inherited patterns. Different methods fit one history.
scenes.caption: Now bring the lanes together. Gold fossils show change through time. Blue DNA places whales on a mammal branch. Green anatomy and teal development preserve inherited patterns. Different methods fit one history.
scenes.visual: Rebuild the centered white tree. Gold, blue, green, and teal lanes slide beside it, each ending in its own check-shaped marker. Keep the lanes separate and never combine them into a proof badge.
scenes.narration: Now bring the lanes together. Gold fossils show change through time. Blue DNA places whales on a mammal branch. Green anatomy and teal development preserve inherited patterns. Different methods fit one history.

scenes.tts: Agreement is not certainty, and each test has limits. Fossil sequences do not identify direct parents. Similarity matters only for comparable DNA. A useful structure can still record ancestry.
scenes.caption: Agreement is not certainty, and each test has limits. Fossil sequences do not identify direct parents. Similarity matters only for comparable DNA. A useful structure can still record ancestry.
scenes.visual: Keep the four lanes moving. Under gold, add 'not direct parents'; under blue, 'compare matching regions'; under green, 'function may remain'. Use full-opacity concept colors and no red rejection marks.
scenes.narration: Agreement is not certainty, and each test has limits. Fossil sequences do not identify direct parents. Similarity matters only for comparable DNA. A useful structure can still record ancestry.

scenes.tts: A scientific theory is a tested explanation that connects many observations. Evolution predicts related patterns before each evidence lane is opened. Confidence grows when those patterns appear across methods, not because any label says proof.
scenes.caption: A scientific theory is a tested explanation that connects many observations. Evolution predicts related patterns before each evidence lane is opened. Confidence grows when those patterns appear across methods, not because any label says proof.
scenes.visual: Rewind the four lane endings to question marks, then reveal their separate check-shaped markers again in sequence. Keep the white tree unchanged and show no word or badge reading 'proof'.
scenes.narration: A scientific theory is a tested explanation that connects many observations. Evolution predicts related patterns before each evidence lane is opened. Confidence grows when those patterns appear across methods, not because any label says proof.

scenes.tts: Each method could have pointed to another history. Instead, their patterns agree within their limits. Independent evidence that agrees strengthens an explanation of common descent.
scenes.caption: Each method could have pointed to another history. Instead, their patterns agree within their limits. Independent evidence that agrees strengthens an explanation of common descent.
scenes.visual: The four colored lanes settle around the large white whale-hippo tree. A soft outline grows around the whole evidence picture while every lane remains distinct and gently moving.
scenes.narration: Each method could have pointed to another history. Instead, their patterns agree within their limits. Independent evidence that agrees strengthens an explanation of common descent.

scenes.visual: Show one line only: 'Independent evidence that agrees strengthens an explanation of common descent.' Keep the four colored lanes moving faintly behind it.
